modules.name: Traffic impact and mobility visualization
modules.effort: M for the static tier (v1); L for the simulation tier (roadmap)
modules.design_question: What do the tower's vehicle, servicing and drop-off trips add to adjacent intersections and lanes at peak, and where do queues or conflicts reach pedestrians, cyclists or transit?
inputs: Vehicle peak-hour trips from P09-M01 or P09-M07
ServicingPlan access points and truck schedule from P09-M05
Optional: pedestrian band results from P09-M04
Street network from OpenStreetMap (OSMnx) and City open data (public streets, lanes, one-way streets, bikeways, truck routes)
User-supplied background volumes, signal timings (cycle length, walk interval), 15-minute PHF and lane geometry
TransLink screenline counts (2011, 2017) for background growth, time-of-day shape and truck share context
Rapid-transit stations and lines

parameters.name: Added peak-hour vehicle volume by approach
parameters.relationship: Higher added volume raises v/c and control delay at the receiving intersection, moving LOS toward E or F as critical v/c approaches 0.85 to 1.0.

parameters.name: Signal cycle length and green split
parameters.relationship: More green for the loaded movement raises its capacity and cuts its delay, but a longer cycle lengthens the maximum pedestrian wait (cycle length minus walk interval). Check pedestrian waits beside vehicle LOS.

parameters.name: Trip distribution to approaches (set by access position)
parameters.relationship: Access on a lane near an arterial pushes more turns onto that intersection; access on a side street spreads turns but loads a quieter street.

parameters.name: Background traffic, growth, time-of-day shape and 15-minute PHF
parameters.relationship: Higher background volume or a more peaked PHF leaves less spare capacity, so the same tower trips cause a larger delay increase. Screenline data show CBD traffic +10% (2011-2017) and hourly shape; City counts are historical or link-only.

parameters.name: Truck share of background traffic
parameters.relationship: More trucks lower saturation flow and raise delay at the access intersection. Regional screenlines: about 4% of vehicles (2017, 24 h) and about 6% (2011, 16 h), highest at midday; not a site value.

parameters.name: Pedestrian and cyclist crossing volumes
parameters.relationship: More crossings at a curb cut or intersection raise conflict exposure and cut vehicle capacity during crossing phases.

parameters.name: Bikeway type on adjacent streets
parameters.relationship: Protected or AAA bikeways beside access points add conflict points and may need driveway redesign. The bikeways dataset carries type and AAA flags.

parameters.name: Taxi, ride-hail and delivery vehicle share
parameters.relationship: More ride-hail and delivery vehicles raise kerb occupancy and add trips even when parking supply is small. Scales with P09-M01 and P09-M05 outputs.

parameters.name: Transit stations and frequency near the site
parameters.relationship: Nearby rapid-transit stations and short headways support a higher transit share in P09-M01. The City dataset gives 22 station points; headways come from GTFS for the proxy station's lines.

metrics.name: Intersection control delay band (HCM-style LOS), descriptive
metrics.good: 55 s or less (LOS A-D) shown green as a descriptive band; no pass/fail badge
metrics.bad: LOS E (55-80 s) amber and LOS F (over 80 s) red as descriptive bands; acceptability of any LOS is a human judgement
metrics.value_status: sourced (S18 Table 3-3, HCM 2000; later-edition bands reported unchanged, unverified)
metrics.flag_ref: r1 TEAM_ASSUMPTION: LOS D acceptable (now context only)
metrics.basis: Delay bands match FHWA Table 3-3. Round 2 removes LOS D as a pass line because Vancouver ranks walking, cycling and transit first; the LOS F v/c override is a separate metric.
metrics.method: Control delay from signal timing and volumes, then banded; label 'HCM-style (bands unchanged in later editions, unverified)'.

metrics.name: LOS F override: lane-group v/c above 1.0
metrics.good: No lane group above 1.0
metrics.bad: Any lane group above 1.0 is shown LOS F
metrics.value_status: unverified (expert-stated for later HCM editions; not in S18)
metrics.basis: S18 assigns F by delay above 80 s only; the override is split out so it cannot lend its status to the delay bands.
metrics.method: Check lane-group v/c from saturation flow and green split.

metrics.name: Critical volume-to-capacity ratio
metrics.good: Below 0.85 (under capacity)
metrics.bad: Above 1.00 (demand exceeds capacity); 0.85-0.95 near capacity (amber), 0.95-1.00 unstable flow (red-amber)
metrics.value_status: sourced (S18 Table 3-2, Quick Estimation Method, HCM 2000 edition)
metrics.basis: Table 3-2 splits near capacity (0.85-0.95) from unstable flow (0.95-1.00); section 3.3.5's single 0.85-1.00 band is not used. Edition currency versus later HCM not checked.
metrics.method: Volume over capacity for the critical movement, banded with Table 3-2.

metrics.name: Pedestrian crossing wait at intersections serving the plaza
metrics.unit: s (maximum wait = cycle length minus walk interval)
metrics.good: Shorter than the vehicle control delay at the same intersection (mode-priority comparison, no absolute threshold)
metrics.bad: Longer than the vehicle control delay at the same intersection
metrics.value_status: assumed (arithmetic from user timings; HCM pedestrian delay formula not opened)
metrics.basis: FHWA chapter 3 puts pedestrian LOS outside its scope; the 1997 hierarchy (S12) puts pedestrians first.
metrics.method: Cycle length minus walk interval, from user-entered signal timings; shown beside vehicle LOS.

metrics.name: Queue spill from the site access onto the street
metrics.good: 0 m
metrics.bad: Any spill
metrics.basis: Geometric preset; storage from P09-M05; simulated queue from SimPy (MIT) in P09-M05.
metrics.method: Simulated 95th-percentile queue minus storage length.

metrics.name: Mode-priority check
metrics.good: No mitigation worsens pedestrian band, crossing wait, cycling or transit access in order to cut vehicle delay
metrics.bad: Any such trade-off
metrics.value_status: sourced (1997 hierarchy as reported by Memon 2009)
metrics.basis: The 1997 hierarchy (pedestrians, cyclists, transit, goods, then cars) may be superseded.
metrics.method: Compare P09-M04 bands, crossing waits and bikeway conflicts before and after mitigation.

visualization: Map with street edges coloured by v/c on a diverging 0-1.2 scale with ticks at 0.85, 0.95 and 1.0, and intersections as discs sized by delay and coloured by LOS A (green) to F (red) as descriptive bands
Difference map (with minus without project) of delay in seconds
deck.gl animated trips layer for simulation output with queue bars at site access (roadmap tier)
Mode-priority panel showing pedestrian bands, crossing waits (seconds) and bikeway conflicts beside vehicle LOS
Chord diagram of project trips by origin zone and mode
outputs: IntersectionPerformance {id, volume, v/c, delay, LOS, pedestrian_max_wait} with and without project
NetworkFlowDelta (GeoJSON edges)
QueueSpillFlags for P09-M05 and PUBL
SimulationConfig (SUMO files) for reuse by forks
modules.method: Tier 1, static: distribute project peak-hour vehicle trips onto approaches using access positions and shortest paths on the OSM network; add background volumes (screenline growth and hourly shape as context); compute v/c per movement from saturation flow and green split and delay with HCM-style terms using user timings; classify delay with the FHWA/HCM bands as descriptive colours and report the lane-group v/c override separately (expert-stated, unverified). Report pedestrian maximum wait (cycle minus walk interval) beside vehicle delay. Tier 2, simulation (roadmap): export network and demand to SUMO (netconvert) or UXsim and read edge delays and queues from detectors, with-project versus without-project. A mode-priority check reads pedestrian bands from P09-M04 and flags mitigation that trades pedestrian comfort for vehicle delay. The 15-minute PHF is an explicit input. Placeholder signal data are labelled.
modules.human_judgment: How much vehicle delay to accept against pedestrian, cycle and transit priority, whether to propose street changes, how to narrate impact in the policy reflection, and whether assumed signal timings are credible.
modules.limits: City data are link-only intersection counts (2020) and 2004-2013 counters in a legacy tool; screenline counts are regional and 2011/2017. No signal timings or lane widths. HCM is paywalled, so delay formulas are generic and HCM 2000 bands may differ from later editions. The site is hypothetical, so trips are scenario inputs. Microsimulation needs calibration; results are comparative, not a traffic impact study.

flags.claim: Downtown Vancouver, or any Vancouver site, must provide a minimum number of off-street parking spaces.
flags.correction: No minimum parking applies for any use citywide since 30 June 2024; the downtown peninsula was exempt from 2018. Accessible, visitor, bicycle and loading spaces are still required.
flags.detail: Sources S01 and S02 (opened) agree. The Province's TOA rules also bar required residential parking near rapid transit (S24). The tool must never score a parking shortfall as a deficiency. [r3 note: S01 gives no effective date; the 30 June 2024 date comes from S02.]

flags.claim: The 2023 Trip Diary weekday shares for CBD sub-regions 21 and 22 are the right default mode split for all trips the tower generates (office, retail, hotel, residential).
flags.correction: Use residence-based shares for residential trips and destination-based shares (trips ending in the CBD: Census place-of-work, City cordon counts or a dashboard destination filter) for attraction uses. Store basis, sample size and confidence interval with each loaded share and flag attraction runs on a residence-based share (r2: watermark, not block).
flags.detail: The survey recruits and weights households by residence sub-area (S15 weighting exhibit uses household and person controls by sub seed; sub-regions 21 and 22 have household sample targets of a few hundred each). The shares therefore describe trips by CBD residents, not workers and visitors arriving from across the region. Evidence: S15 (opened, text extracted); S16. [r3 note: the round-1 wording that the diary 'cannot give' destination splits and that S16 lists no destination product was itself false; see the r3 flag on destination tabulation.]

flags.claim: TfL Pedestrian Comfort Level bands are verified thresholds for peak-minute flows in below-grade station passages, with B+ (11 ppmm or less) good and 18 ppmm or more bad for all area types.
flags.correction: Use TfL only for street footways and crossings, on peak-hour flow (people per hour / 60 / clear width), against the Figure 9 acceptability table by area type. Use station methods (TCQSM chapter 10 walkway and queuing scales) for passages, stairs and fare lines. Status: team_assumption.
flags.detail: S17 (opened, text extracted): scope is footways and crossings; ppmm is people per hour divided by 60 and by clear width, calculated for average, peak-hour and Average of Maximum Activity flows. Multiplying hourly flow by a platoon factor and reading hour-average bands double-counts peaking. [r2 note: the round-1 wording here about the C+ floor and the cell-level Figure 9 reading was superseded by the r2 flag on Figure 9; C+ is the limit on the vitality exception, not a general fail line.]

flags.claim: Queue area per person of 1.4 m2 or more is Fruin LOS A-C and below 0.9 m2 is LOS E-F at stairs and fare lines.
flags.correction: 1.4 and 0.9 m2 per person are walkway-scale boundaries (C/D and D/E). Queues use a separate queuing-area scale (reviewer: A 1.2 or more, B 0.9-1.2, C 0.7-0.9, D 0.3-0.7, E 0.2-0.3, F under 0.2 m2 per person). Keep both scales and cite the exhibit once read.
flags.detail: Reviewer expert knowledge of Fruin (1971) as reproduced in TCQSM 3rd ed. ch.10. The primary copy could not be opened (S44 reader page has no table text, re-tried in r2; the PDF exceeds the fetch size limit), so both scales stay unverified and bounds such as 0.65 versus 0.7 m2 may differ by edition.

flags.claim: Peak headways relevant to the station are Expo 2-5 min, Millennium 3-4 min and Canada 6 min.
flags.correction: For a CBD station use the Expo trunk (about 2-3 min combined) and the Canada Line trunk (about 3 min combined), read from GTFS for the actual station. The Millennium Line terminates at VCC-Clark and is excluded.
flags.detail: S23 (re-opened): Expo 2-5 min is the line's own frequency and 2-3 min combined on shared track; Millennium runs VCC-Clark to Lafarge Lake-Douglas and is not shown serving Waterfront since 2016; Canada Line 6 min is its own branch frequency and 3 min combined on the trunk. [r2 note: the correction above was itself incomplete; see the r2 flag on combining both trunks at one station.]

flags.claim: FHWA Table 3-2 gives v/c bands of under 0.85 stable, 0.85-1.00 near capacity and over 1.00 oversaturated.
flags.correction: Cite Table 3-2 exactly: under 0.85, 0.85-0.95 near capacity, 0.95-1.00 unstable flow, over 1.00 demand exceeds capacity. The single 0.85-1.00 band is from section 3.3.5. Add the reviewer-stated LOS F override for lane-group v/c above 1.0 (later HCM editions; unverified) and label the method HCM-style.
flags.detail: S18 re-opened (r1 and r2): Table 3-2 lists under 0.85, 0.85-0.95, 0.95-1.00 and over 1.00 (HCM 2000 Quick Estimation Method). The page does not map v/c above 1.0 to LOS F; Table 3-3 assigns LOS F by delay above 80 s only.

flags.claim: VTPI TDM reduction ranges (4-20%, about 15%, 34-37%, 35%) are verified thresholds for claimed reductions at a downtown Vancouver tower.
flags.correction: Treat them as team-applied evidence ranges with an 'evidence context: US metro / predicted' label on each value.
flags.detail: S19 re-opened: the 35% and 20% figures are Ewing 1993 Sacramento model predictions; 34-37% is measured against ITE average trip rates in Minneapolis-St Paul (Spack and Finkelstein 2014); 4-20% is Rye and Boarnet worksite programmes; 15% versus 7% is a four-metro US survey. [r2 note: the round-1 remedy of scaling these by k = site auto share / evidence auto share was itself false; see the r2 flag.]

flags.claim: ITE trip rates do not consider location, so local survey data are the only option for downtown sites.
